title: Citation Graphs Over Time
answer: Citation graphs over time are directed networks in which each node is a research work and each edge is a citation, with a timestamp that records when the citing work appeared. sections.body: Citation graphs over time are directed networks in which each node is a research work and each edge is a citation, with a timestamp that records when the citing work appeared. The scope covers citation counts, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, temporal paths, burst detection, and the rise and fall of research communities. It also covers how fields split, merge, and borrow methods across decades. On this site, the library of 135 research papers can be represented as a small citation graph over time, which makes the topic concrete rather than abstract.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on bibliographic metadata, reference lists, and persistent identifiers such as DOIs, gathered from publisher sites, open citation indexes, and library catalogues. Storage often uses a graph database for edges and a relational or column store for paper metadata, with object storage for full texts and snapshots. Compute ranges from a single machine running NetworkX or igraph to a cluster running batch graph processing. Versioned snapshots matter because a citation graph changes as new papers appear and as older records are corrected.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners ingest metadata, resolve references, deduplicate author and paper records, and build nodes and edges with timestamps. They then slice the graph by year or month, compute centrality, PageRank, and community structure, and compare those measures across time. Temporal path analysis traces how an idea moves from one paper to another, while burst detection flags sudden increases in citations to a work or topic. Visual tools such as Gephi or custom notebooks help inspect the resulting structures, and the output is usually a set of metrics, tables, and interactive views.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk depend on the source of the citation data, because publisher terms, database licences, and open citation licences differ. Provenance records the source database, the retrieval date, the query, and every normalization or disambiguation step, so that a later analyst can reproduce the graph. Risks include incomplete reference lists, author name ambiguity, citation cartels, coercive citation, and the persistence of retracted works in historical graphs. Good practice keeps a clear audit trail and separates raw records from derived edges and metrics.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward open citation data, real-time updates, and richer links between citation edges and the claims, methods, and datasets inside papers. Temporal knowledge graphs and dynamic embeddings aim to represent how influence shifts without collapsing history into a single snapshot. On this site, the 11795 claims extracted from research works could be attached to citation edges, so a reader can see not only who cited whom but which specific claims travelled. Expect more integration with model and tool catalogues, and more attention to provenance as graphs grow.
